article.overview: A gravimeter measures the acceleration due to gravity at one place, and changes in that acceleration over time. On the Moon, a surface gravimeter can check local gravity, record how the ground responds to tidal forces and, in principle, detect very weak vibrations. The only flown surface gravimeter in the sources read is the Apollo 17 Lunar Surface Gravimeter (LSG), deployed by the astronauts on 12 December 1972. Its design goals were not fully met because of a suspended-mass problem found after deployment and later thermal control faults, and its record is now used mainly as a seismometer. The orbital counterpart is the GRAIL mission, whose twin spacecraft mapped the lunar gravity field from lunar orbit in 2011 and 2012. Scope: this article covers instruments that measure local gravitational acceleration with a sensor on the lunar surface, and orbital mapping of the lunar gravity field as the principal lunar gravity measurement. GRAIL's instrument is a ranging system rather than a surface gravimeter.
article.description: Gravity is the force that pulls an object towards a massive body. A gravimeter measures the acceleration produced by that force, in metres per second squared, or in gal where 1 gal is 1 cm/s squared. The Apollo 17 LSG's nominal sensitivity is stated as one part in 10 to the power 11 of lunar gravity, which is a design figure and not a measured result. Gravimeters fall into two families. A relative gravimeter measures changes in gravity between places or times with a mechanical spring-mass system. An absolute gravimeter measures the full gravity value by timing a freely falling test mass against length and time standards. The Apollo 17 LSG was a relative spring-mass instrument. Modern Earth-based absolute gravimeters use free fall and laser interferometry. Cold-atom and superconducting instruments have been proposed, but the sources read do not describe a lunar surface design for either type. The LSG was designed to cover the vertical component of gravity from zero (steady gravity and slow tidal change) up to 16 Hz, which includes seismic and gravitational-radiation interest. That band overlaps the seismometer band, which is why the instrument was later studied as a seismometer.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The stated objectives of the Apollo 17 LSG were to measure lunar surface gravitational acceleration and its temporal variations, determine lunar gravity relative to Earth gravity, measure surface deformation due to tidal forces, measure vertical lunar seismicity, and monitor free oscillations of the Moon that gravitational radiation from cosmic sources might induce. The instrument was also meant to be correlated with gravimeters on Earth to search for gravitational radiation. Several of these objectives relate to the Moon's interior: tidal deformation is a measure of the body's response to tidal forces, and seismic and free-oscillation signals travel through the interior. The sources read do not draw a conclusion about the interior from the LSG record, and they do not report a measured lunar gravity value or tidal amplitude from the LSG. The orbital GRAIL mission was designed to map the gravity field so that scientists could study the Moon's interior from crust to core. Its gravity model resolves small surface features such as tectonic structures, volcanic landforms, basin rings and crater central peaks. Cold-atom gravity sensors have been studied for Earth-observation gravity gradiometry; the sources read do not describe a lunar surface version.
article.operating_principle: Apollo 17 LSG (spring-mass relative gravimeter): the instrument used a LaCoste-Romberg-type sensing arrangement. A horizontal beam is held level by a zero-length spring, whose restoring force is directly proportional to its length. A mass suspended from the beam by a second spring balances the beam's weight. A plate on the free end of the beam sits midway between two fixed capacitor plates when the beam is exactly horizontal. If gravity changes, the beam moves and the capacitor plates produce an alternating-current error voltage. That voltage can be amplified and fed back to the plates to restore the beam to level; the feedback signal is the output. The spring was held near 323 K and controlled to better than one millidegree, using insulation, a heater, a sunshield and a hole in the top of the housing that radiated heat to the dark sky. GRAIL (orbital gravity mapping): gravity was recovered indirectly. Two spacecraft flew in formation, and their separation changed as they passed over areas of different gravity. An instrument on each spacecraft measured the change in their relative velocity, and the gravity field was recovered from that tracking record. The measuring instrument was the Lunar Gravity Ranging System. Absolute free-fall gravimeters (comparison only): in an Earth-based absolute gravimeter a reflector is dropped in vacuum and a laser interferometer counts interference fringes as it falls, giving the trajectory and the gravity value. A reference reflector on an inertial isolation system measures ground vibration, which is the main error source. The FG5 is cited by its manufacturer as having a measurement accuracy of 2 microgal. Cold-atom gravity sensors (comparison only): a cold-atom interferometer uses cooled atoms as matter waves; in a space gradiometer two atom interferometers act as a differential accelerometer, and the phase difference gives a gravity gradient. The sources read describe this only as a proposed Earth-orbit concept.
article.scientific_importance: The Apollo 17 LSG was designed to connect surface gravity, tides and seismic signals in one instrument. In practice, as far as the sources read show, its most useful product was the seismic record. Kawamura and colleagues showed that LSG data could be used as a lunar seismometer. They reported that the malfunction's effect was small and that the recorded signals were consistent with the other Apollo seismometers, and they used the data to examine deep moonquake nests. A later abstract describes efforts to recover LSG data that had been lost, including data from April to June 1975. GRAIL's gravity model is important for the whole Moon: it resolves small surface features, and its stated aim was to probe the interior from crust to core. Its results are based on tracking data rather than a surface measurement, so they complement surface instruments without replacing them. A surface gravimeter measures gravity and its change at one place with high time resolution. An orbital mission maps the global field with spatial resolution set by orbit altitude and tracking.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, power or sensitivity for a gravimeter. The Apollo 17 LSG and the GRAIL mission are different types of system, so the values below are tied to each named instrument or mission and its source. Where a value is not stated in the sources read, the article says so, and no value has been estimated.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Surface Gravimeter (LSG)
examples.type: Lunar surface relative spring-mass gravimeter (ALSEP experiment S-207)
examples.status: Flown (lunar surface). Deployed by the Apollo 17 astronauts on 12 December 1972 about 8 m from the ALSEP central station. Principal investigator Joseph Weber, University of Maryland, with J. V. Larson.
examples.description: A LaCoste-Romberg gravimeter with electronics, spring-mass suspension capacitor plates, a sunshield and a ribbon cable to the ALSEP central station. Total mass of the basic equipment, including gravimeter, electronics, sensors, sunshield and ribbon cable, is 12.7 kg. Average power 9.3 W and average bit rate 0.59625 kbit/s, according to the NSSDC record.
examples.frequency_coverage: Three bands from 0 (DC) to 16 Hz. Lowest band from DC to one cycle per 20 minutes (lunar tides); middle band from one cycle per 20 minutes to three cycles per minute; highest band from three cycles per minute to 16 Hz (seismic and gravitational-radiation interest).
examples.sensitivity: Nominal sensitivity of one part in 10^11 of lunar gravity (design figure; no measured noise floor given in the sources read).
examples.thermal_control: Spring optimal temperature about 323 K, controlled to better than one millidegree; sunshield, insulation, radiating hole to dark sky and a heater.
examples.operating_record: After deployment the balance mass was found too light and rested against its upper stop; the beam could not be balanced even with all available extra mass added by ground command. The beam was centred by an extra load of 140 mg (about 0.0017 N) applied by partial caging of the mass-weight assembly. In that state the instrument behaved as a gravimeter with a resonant frequency of 1.5 Hz and a post-amplifier gain of 17. Ground commands were used over the following year and a half to reconfigure settings. The heater regulation circuit failed in the full-on position on 15 March 1974 (data unusable until 20 April 1974) and again on 7 July 1975; temperature stability returned on 2 September 1975. The NSSDC record notes that the regulation problem recurred on 19 September 1975 and that the record does not resolve how much usable data followed. Useful data continued until ALSEP shutdown on 30 September 1977.
examples.measured_result: The sources read do not report a measured lunar gravity value, tidal amplitude or gravitational-wave limit from the LSG.
examples.dimensions_status: Not stated in the PDS overview or NSSDC record read.

examples.name: GRAIL gravity-field mapping (Ebb and Flow, Lunar Gravity Ranging System)
examples.type: Lunar orbital gravity-field mapping by spacecraft tracking (not a surface gravimeter)
examples.status: Flown in lunar orbit. Twin spacecraft Ebb (GRAIL-A) and Flow (GRAIL-B) were launched on 10 September 2011 and were powered down and impacted the Moon on 17 December 2012.
examples.description: The gravity field was recovered from changes in the distance and relative velocity between the two spacecraft. The measuring instrument was the Lunar Gravity Ranging System (LGRS).
examples.gravity_model: Zuber et al. (2013) model reported as GL0420A, extending to degree and order 420, corresponding to a spatial block size of about 13 km. This is a secondary summary; the primary paper was not read in full.
examples.science_results: The gravity model resolves tectonic structures, volcanic landforms, basin rings, crater central peaks and many simple bowl-shaped craters.
examples.specifications_status: Mass, power, dimensions and LGRS design not stated in the sources read.

examples.type: Proposed concept (Earth-focused; not flown; no lunar design found)
examples.status: Proposed. The 2019 concept study describes a space gravity gradiometer for mapping Earth's gravitational field.
examples.description: Cold-atom interferometers used as a differential accelerometer configuration to measure gravity gradients.
examples.specifications_status: No numerical sensitivity, mass or power stated in the abstract read.

examples.name: Lunar Gravitational-wave Antenna (LGWA) concept
examples.type: Proposed concept (seismic-type inertial vibration sensors; not a gravimeter)
examples.status: Proposed. A 2020 concept paper describes monitoring of the Moon's vibrational eigenmodes excited by gravitational waves.
examples.description: Inertial vibration sensors for monitoring the Moon's elastic vibrations, in the millihertz band suggested by Weber. The abstract does not state the sensor count, network layout, sensitivity or mass.
examples.specifications_status: Not stated in the abstract read.

physical_specifications.comparison_note: The examples measure different quantities: the Apollo LSG measures local gravity acceleration and its change at one place; GRAIL measures the global gravity field from orbit; the cold-atom concept is a gradient instrument for Earth; LGWA is a seismic-type concept. No comparison table is given because the values are not comparable. The Apollo LSG is the only example with a published mass and power figure.
physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo 17 LSG's dimensions are not stated in the PDS overview or the NSSDC record read. The GRAIL spacecraft and LGRS dimensions are not stated in the sources read. The cold-atom and LGWA concepts have no dimensions in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Apollo 17 LSG: total mass 12.7 kg for the basic equipment including gravimeter, electronics, sensors, sunshield and ribbon cable (PDS overview; NSSDC record). GRAIL spacecraft and LGRS mass: not stated in the sources read.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Apollo 17 LSG: average power 9.3 W (NSSDC record). The PDS overview does not give a power figure. GRAIL and the concept examples: not stated in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The Apollo 17 LSG had to stay in a narrow thermal range: its spring operated near 323 K and had to be held to better than one millidegree over the lunar day-night cycle. The design used a sunshield, insulation, a hole in the top of the housing to radiate heat to the dark sky, and a heater. Its thermal failures in 1974 and 1975 show how sensitive the design was to these controls. The LSG was levelled and aligned using a sunshield shadow, within plus or minus three degrees, and a ribbon cable connected it to the ALSEP central station electronics. Because the instrument's spring and mass respond to ground motion, vibration is treated as a signal in the seismic-use analysis; Earth-based absolute gravimeters use a reference reflector on an isolation system to handle the same problem. The orbital GRAIL mission has no surface thermal requirement, and its tracking and operating requirements are not described in the sources read.
article.limitations: A surface gravimeter measures gravity at one point and cannot map the field over a region. The Apollo 17 LSG's suspended mass was too light for the beam to balance after deployment, and the fix used a 140 mg load applied through caging, which changed the instrument's behaviour. The sources read do not state how the resulting 1.5 Hz resonant frequency affected the gravity measurement, and the instrument was used mainly as a one-axis vertical seismometer. Its operating life was also limited by thermal faults, which left the instrument without usable data for several weeks in 1974 and disrupted the record in 1975. Orbital gravity mapping is limited by orbit altitude, tracking quality and the number of passes; the GRAIL resolution applies to its own orbit. No lunar-surface cold-atom or quantum gravimeter was found in the sources read; the concepts found are for Earth or are seismic-type proposals.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The Apollo 17 LSG was carried to the Moon on the Apollo 17 mission as an ALSEP-linked experiment and was deployed by the astronauts about 8 m from the ALSEP central station. GRAIL's twin spacecraft were launched in 2011 and operated in lunar orbit until December 2012. No compatibility is asserted for any named lander, rover or spacecraft.
transportation_process: Apollo 17 surface: the LSG was delivered to the surface on the Apollo 17 mission. The sources read do not describe its stowage on the lunar module or the release sequence in detail.
Apollo 17 surface deployment: on 12 December 1972 the astronauts levelled and aligned the instrument within plus or minus three degrees using the sunshield shadow.
Apollo 17 surface: the ribbon cable was mated to the ALSEP central station electronics.

GRAIL orbit: twin spacecraft launched 10 September 2011 and operated in lunar orbit until 17 December 2012. The cruise, orbit-insertion and commissioning sequences are not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 17 LSG: crewed, hand-deployed installation beside the ALSEP central station, with levelling and alignment by sunshield shadow and a ribbon cable connection [1][3]. GRAIL: no surface deployment; the instrument operated from lunar orbit via spacecraft tracking [6][7].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 LSG is the historical example of a surface gravimeter in the sources read. GRAIL is the historical example of orbital gravity-field mapping by spacecraft tracking. The Apollo method is historical and does not show how a future surface gravimeter would be delivered.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility is asserted with any named lander, rover or spacecraft. Any future gravimeter would need its mass, dimensions, mounting interface, thermal requirements, power, data rate and deployment method checked against verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 LSG was deployed in December 1972. No earlier lunar surface gravimeter was found in the sources read. Its designed objectives were not fully met, but its record was later used to examine deep moonquake nests and to locate new ones. GRAIL's gravity model, published in 2013, is the lunar gravity field reference cited here for the orbital method; the sources read do not assess its influence on later work. Cold-atom and quantum gravity sensors are an active area of study, but the sources read show no lunar-surface flight or funded lunar-surface design.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Key uncertainties: the Apollo 17 LSG's dimensions are not published in the sources read; the post-1975 data quality is uncertain because the NSSDC record says regulation problems recurred in September 1975 while also stating that useful data continued until 1977; no measured gravity value, tidal amplitude or gravitational-wave limit from the LSG is reported in the sources read; the Kawamura et al. (2015) statements come from an abstract read through a search summary, and a 2017 abstract gives a different count of nest locations. The GRAIL gravity-model details come from a secondary summary, and the primary paper was not read in full. The LGWA and cold-atom concepts were read from abstracts only, and neither gives a numerical sensitivity in the abstract read.

Direct image URLs were checked with HTTP requests returning 200 and image content types. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. data_quality_notes: Scope: this article covers local gravity-acceleration sensors placed on the lunar surface (the Apollo 17 LSG being the only flown example found) and orbital mapping of the lunar gravity field as the principal lunar gravity measurement (GRAIL). GRAIL's instrument is a ranging system rather than a surface gravimeter. Payload 017 (gravity gradiometer), 025 (tidal deformation sensor) and 001 to 004 (seismometers) are cross-referenced and not repeated.

Apollo 17 LSG deployment date: the PDS overview and the NSSDC record both give 12 December 1972. A NASA-hosted LGWA document cited in a search summary gives 1977, which appears to refer to a different event. The 1972 date is used.
Apollo 17 LSG dimensions are not stated in the PDS overview or the NSSDC record read. No dimension value is given.

Apollo 17 LSG post-1975 performance is uncertain: the NSSDC record says the regulation problem recurred on 19 September 1975 and also states that useful data continued until the ALSEP shutdown on 30 September 1977. The record does not resolve how much usable data followed.

Apollo 17 LSG measured results: no measured lunar gravity value, tidal amplitude or gravitational-wave limit from the LSG is reported in the sources read. The nominal sensitivity of one part in 10^11 is a design figure.
Apollo 17 LSG full technical report (NASA SP-330, Chapter 12) and the 1974 Larson and Weber report were not read in full. The PDS overview and the NTRS abstract were the main sources.

Kawamura et al. (2015): read through a search summary; the publisher DOI returned HTTP 403 to curl. The statements about the malfunction's effect, the deep moonquake nests examined and the new nests located come from that summary. A 2017 AGU abstract gives a different count of nest locations; the difference is unresolved.
2017 AGU abstract (Phillips et al., P41D-2859): seen in a search summary only; the ADS page returned HTTP 405 to curl. Its data-recovery statement (April to June 1975) is not verified in full.

GRAIL: the primary paper (Zuber et al., 2013, Science, DOI 10.1126/science.1231507) was not read in full because the publisher page returned HTTP 403. Volume and page numbers are not verified. The gravity-model statement (GL0420A, degree and order 420, about 13 km block size) comes from a secondary course handout.
GRAIL spacecraft and LGRS mass, power, dimensions and design are not stated in the sources read. The sources read do not describe the GRAIL cruise, orbit-insertion or commissioning sequences.

Cold-atom gravity sensors: the 2019 concept (Trimeche et al.) was read from its abstract only and is Earth-focused, with no numerical sensitivity in the abstract. No lunar-surface cold-atom or quantum gravimeter design, budget or funded mission was found. A concept named LANGO (superconducting accelerometers) appeared in a search summary but was not read in primary form, so it is not used.
LGWA (Harms et al., 2020): read from the abstract only. The abstract gives no sensor count, network layout, band or sensitivity. LGWA is a seismic-type concept rather than a gravimeter.
Superconducting and other Earth-based gravimeters: not researched beyond the free-fall principle and the FG5 accuracy figure quoted from the manufacturer. They are not described in detail.

Images: the two Apollo 17 LSG images are direct Wikimedia Commons assets (verified HTTP 200 with image content types and visually checked), not NASA catalogue pages. The Apollo frame number of the deployed photograph was not confirmed, and the original NASA figure for the structure diagram was not located. The Commons rights statements (public domain, NASA-created) were recorded but not independently verified against NASA's copyright policy. Because the Apollo images are not from an official NASA page, direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is set to false. The GRAIL map is a NASA Photojournal asset (verified HTTP 200); its credit line is reported as NASA/ARC/MIT in a search summary, but was not confirmed on the fetched HTML.
The Apollo 17 LSG deployment is described only relative to the ALSEP central station (about 8 m away). No lunar landing-site or location recommendation is made, as deferred by the user.
No compatibility claim is made for any named lander, rover or spacecraft. The transportation section describes the historical Apollo deployment and the GRAIL orbital operations only.
